records.Etymology: 300. Kann. kár ‘sheep’, Rp. kar ‘ram; billy goat’, Bun. kar ‘sheep (male, castrated)’ — cf. Ind. kʌ́rū ‘lion, tiger; wild sheep’ with many parallels in languages in the northwest (loc.cit.); also Kann. byaṅ kar(h) ‘Tibetan ram’, Par. ɣarȭ ‘sheep’, Sak. kaura- ‘sheep’, Wkh. kar ‘mouton à courtes oreilles’, Bur. kíro ‘sheep (child’s language)’, karéelo ‘ram’, Sh.chil. kará̄ ‘a ram’ — Bhil. karᵃḍu and M. karaḍũ̄ both ‘kid’. As I have pointed out (2005: 103) the word might be of Dravidian origin, e.g., Tam. koṟi ‘sheep’ (cf. DEDR 1799 for Dravidian alloforms and semantic varieties similar to those of Northern Pakistan), whereas Harold Walter Bailey suggests derivation < PIE *kapro- ‘he-goat’ (1979: 65). But cf. also Čašule’s suggestion (e.g. 2010: 44) for a PIE background which he supports with reference to Bur. karóoỵo and Sh. karóovo ‘with curved horns’.

records.Etymology: 67. Bng. tɔpkāṇɔ v.t. ‘to grope one’s way, grope along’ (with -k- and -a- suffixes), tɔprāḷ n.m. ‘groping step(s) that lead towards a goal’ (with -rāḷ suffix) and probably tɔpɔ n.m. ‘place or goal within reach, reach, range’, top(i)ṇɔ ‘to guess, figure, feel, touch’ (note topuiɔ pɔriaṇṇɔ ‘to make out or identify by touch or feeling’ [first verb is ABS, second < prájānāti ‘knows, understands’ 8509a]) and pɔrtɔpṇɔ ‘to feel around, grope about’ (with pɔr- prefix), Khaśdh. topiṇa and Deog. tōpṇɔ ‘to grope along’, Old Cam. tōpṇā ‘to look for’, Kann. taptapyá-mig (tap-ta-pyá-mig) ‘to touch, to search for by the touch, to feel or grope for, to seek by feeling’, Pāḍ. and Maṇḍ. tōpṇᵃ ‘to search’ — Ind. tʌ̀p-tʌpʰ karʌ́ṽ ‘to tap, touch lightly’, Bur./Sh. taptáp -̇t- ‘to tap on; tippen an’, and aspirated Ind. thʌ́p-thʌpʰ karʌ́ṽ ‘to grope or feel around in darkness’, Sh.chil. tháp-thap th- ‘to grope around in darkness’, Sh.koh. (RSup) thapȭ vakhat ‘evening’ (second word ← Ar. vaqt ‘time’), Bro. tʰʌptʰup ‘dark’. The aspirated Dard forms appear to be partly contaminated by OIA *thapp- ‘slap, pat’ (6091) – but note also Proto-Khasic *tʰaap ‘to hit, slap’ – whereas the unaspirated WPah. forms may have a parallel in Tam. tappu- ‘to grope, feel about’ (DEDR 2499). We are probably dealing here with a ‘North Indian’ word. Therefore see the following note: Note: A here perhaps related subgroup is this: Pur. ṭʰup ‘dark’ — cf. Bur. ṭumṭáṅ ‘darkness with (or through) dust’ if < older *ṭupṭáṅ (with second sylla- ble ṭaṅ ‘(sky) covered, cloudy, rainy’) — with Bur. are related Sant. ʈamɖao ‘to grope, to feel with hands or feet, as in the dark or in water, to search or try to find in the dark or in water’ (related with ʈamɖa ʈəmɖi ‘to grope, or feel here and there’ and Korwa ʈamɖaːo ‘to grope in the dark’ both of which possibly go back to older *ʈap-) and probably ʈahuʔp ʈaʈuʔp ‘stumbling, floundering, as one walking in the dark; to go slap dash’ (which might derive from older *ʈaʈuʔp ʈaʈuʔp).

records.Etymology: 145. Ind. mʌ̀ṽ ‘a riverbank; a landing place, moorings (at a river bank)’, Kamd. gāl-mól ‘river-bank’, Wg. golmalˈa ‘river bank, valley floor’ (with first word < OIA *ghala- ‘stream’ [4453]), Dm. khoi-má̄li ‘river-bank’ (with first word < OIA *khola- ‘cavity, hollow’ [3943]), Paš. nandə-mālˈa ‘river-bank’ (with first word < OIA nadí̄- ‘river’) and vargamˈāl ‘river-bank’ (with varg(a) < OIA vá̄ri- ‘water, rain’ [11556]) — Orm. ṣʳī-mōl ‘field-embankment’. According to Morgenstierne and accepted by Turner, the Paš. and Dm. forms are < OIA má̄lā- ‘wreath, garland’ (10092). But this is implausi- ble. Therefore alternatively the words derive < PIE *molā ‘shore’ (Pokorny and Köbler but not Mallory and Adams; cf. e.g. Latv. mala ‘edge, bank, border, shore, region’), however contamination by forms related with H. etc. moṛ ‘curve’ (< OIA [ultimately Dravidian móṭati ‘twists’] is possible, cf. Kal. moḷ ‘turn, bend’). Note: See also somewhat similar OIA malaya- and Tam. malai ‘hill, mountain’ (DEDR 4742). Because of Dravidian and Indo-European evidence, Bomhald reconstructs PN *mal-a ‘hill, mountain (CINCL 846). Note, however, also In- scriptional Sanskrit māla- ‘field’ and lex. ‘a forest or wood near a village’, Munda Bodo-Gadaba mala ‘hill field, land cleared for ploughing’ and the synonym form mal biroŋ ‘mountain range’ with further parallels in Mon-Khmer like Brao məːl ‘dry paddy field’, Sapuan mɨəl ‘rice field (wet & dry)’, Tˈin mual ‘plant rice in hill field’.

records.Etymology: 519. (a) Bng. cəś ‘burning pain’, Kc. ċaśiṇo ‘to be burnt (e.g. hand on hot iron)’, Deog. and Jaun. ciśṇɔ ‘to burn one’s hand etc.’, Him. cośṇu ‘to burn with fire’, P. cīs ‘a sharp pain’, Ku. ciśṇō ‘to burn’, ciśi ‘scare of fire’ and cis ‘keen pain, scorching’, cisuk ‘very cold’, N. ciso ‘wet, cold’, Kgr. cas ‘slipped disc’ — Ind. c̣ʌ̀ṣ ‘sudden fierce or stabbing pain; lumbago; a touch’ and c̣ʌ̀s ‘sudden fierce or stabbing pain’, Kal. čičiék ‘to burn or smart (as salt in a wound)’. The words are to be seen in connection (i) with OIA *cassakk- ‘throb, twitch, sudden pain’ (4730), *cīssa- ‘sharp pain’ (4847), caṣati² ‘hurts’ (4727a), chaṣati ‘hurts’ (Dhātup.) (the aspirated form is reflected in Garh. chasāk ‘nukīlī vastu kī halkī cubhan - slight sting or piercing through a pointed object’), cahakk- ‘burn brightly’ (4731) (with debuccalisation), and perhaps cāṣa-  ‘sugarcane’ (4774) (see there G. cās ‘boiled syrup’), and (ii) with OIA *atyuṣati ‘burns’, *atyoṣati, *atyuṣyate ‘is burnt’ (226a), and (iii) perhaps with Dravidian DEDR kiccu (1514): Tam. kiccu ‘fire’, Tel. ciccu ‘fire, flame’ etc. which is perhaps worth comparing with Garh.nā. cac-kār, cac-gār ‘very cold’ (with -kār suffix). The Bng. and Deog. forms go back to older *c̣aṣ-, but not the Kc. form which therefore must be an early borrowing at a time when Proto-Bangāṇī and Proto-Deogārī still had three sibilants but Proto-Kocī only two. See next and next but one. (b) Like in the preceding paragraph, also in this paragraph semantic-morphological amalgamations (see p. 224) have been rampant. Bng. jàṣṇɔ ‘to singe s.o. (e.g., with an iron rod)’, invol. jàśiṇɔ, jìśaiṇɔ ‘to singe o.s. badly’ (with -ai- suffix), Garh. jhās ‘slight neuralgia or birth pangs’, jhasāk ‘touch through fire or nettle’ and jhusmus ‘dawn, early morning’ — here also A. zah ‘heat, summer’? — Pal. jhāṣˈī ‘caterpillar’ (contact with some types causes severe allergic reactions), Tor. j̣eṣ ([jyɛṣ]) ‘caterpillar’, K. zᵃj ‘a certain tiny longish insect, similar to an ant, which by coṅtact with the skin causes irritation and scratching’, Dari. jhusili kirā ‘caterpillar’ and Garh. jhissu or jhijju ‘ek roẽdār kīṛā – a hairy worm’ and jhusalyā ‘person with unwanted hair on his face or body’ and Kho. ǰaláṣ ‘hairy (person); a disheveled, long-haired person’ derive either/or or both < OIA lex. jhaṣa- ‘sun-heat’ (5359) or < OIA *adhyuṣyate ‘is lighted up, burnt’ (280a) with a modern reflex in Kṭg. There is also Bng. ujà̄śɔ n.m. ‘the power that induces spontaneous possession (e.g., during the approaching of a deity towards a village); splendour of the sun’ (with retention of palatal feature because of coronal consonant harmony) which is < related OIA *ujjhāṣa- ‘shining’ (1678) (Pk.) with one modern parallel in G. to which is to be added Br.-Aw. ujās ‘light; gleam’, and Bng. jà̄ś n.f. ‘tension, stress, impulse, cheering up’ which also derives < OIA lex. *jhaṣa- ‘sun-heat’ (5359). (c) Bng. kiśaiṇɔ or ciśaiṇɔ ‘to scorch children in jest with glowing charcoal’ (the lat- ter form is apparently cognate with forms listed in paragraph [a]), Khaś. kreśśnū ͡ and Bhad. ṭlessnū ‘cries due to physical pain’ (Kaul [2006 i: 305]) < OIA *kreśayati ‘presses’ (3606) (but regarding semantics compare cognate OIA kleśayati ‘torments’) with a modern parallel in Dm., but the verb has further parallels in Roh. (3588), Kal. (3589), K. (3590, 3591) and Wg. (3605). Notes: (a) Despite the massive semantic-morphological amalgamations one wonders whether above alternation of Bng. kiśaiṇɔ ∼ ciśaiṇɔ ‘to scorch . . . with glow- ing charcoal’ does not indicate a reflex of OIA KĀŚ ‘shine, look brilliant’ which may be also reflected in Bng. cɔṣṇɔ ‘to light, ignite, burn s.th. or s.o.’, cɔśkɔ i.a. ‘a sudden and short apparition (e.g. of a ghost or of a god in a medium)’ and perhaps in cɔkśɔ, cɔkśelɔ ‘shining, radiant’ if this is reflex of older *caśaka-(illa-) (extended with -kɔ2 suffix [and MIA -illa- suffix). In such a case it could be morphologically compared with OIA cáṣṭe ‘appears’. This interpretations seems semantically more plausible than borrowing from Dravidian. (b) The same OIA root in form of cākṣuṣá- ‘relating to sight’ is perhaps the origin of Kal. čákaš ‘cowrie shell’ which, regarding basic meaning, cf. with Kal. čákaš čhína ‘animal with white mark on its face’ (with second word < OIA cihna- ‘mark, sign’ [4833] and aspiration fronting).
